## TL;DR

**Problem:** Healthcare API platforms handling unpredictable traffic patterns—open enrollment creating large spikes, provider credentialing deadlines driving surges, month-end billing cycles generating increased load, state reporting batch jobs overwhelming shared infrastructure—experience **cascading failures** from uncontrolled request admission causing resource exhaustion (database connection pool exhaustion, out-of-memory crashes, CPU saturation), **unfair resource distribution** where high-volume consumers monopolize capacity impacting low-volume critical workflows (large health systems crowding out solo practitioners, high-population states consuming disproportionate shared capacity), **downstream service overload** violating vendor API rate limits and causing contractual penalties, and **SLA violations** from degraded availability, latency, and error rates. Without capacity-aware throttling, platforms experience recurring resource exhaustion incidents, repeated SLA violations, noisy neighbor incidents, and consumer retry storms that amplify overload.

**Solution:** API Throttling Pattern implements **multi-layered request flow control** through capacity-aware admission control monitoring real-time CPU/memory/database connection/queue depth/downstream health indicators dynamically adjusting admission rates (healthy state CPU <60% admits 100%, degraded 60-75% admits 75% with 25% queued, critical 75-85% admits 50%, overloaded >85% admits critical priority only), **intelligent request queuing** with bounded depth (5,000 requests), configurable TTL (60 seconds standard, 30s critical/300s low priority), and priority-based ordering ensuring critical workflows (P0 emergency, P1 high) maintain access during capacity constraints while bulk operations (P3 low) absorb throttling impact first, **priority-based classification** through HTTP headers (X-Priority), endpoint configuration, consumer tier metadata, and request content analysis enabling 4-tier prioritization (P0 critical emergency healthcare never throttled, P1 high real-time provider operations, P2 normal member portal, P3 low bulk analytics), **backpressure signaling** via HTTP 429 "Too Many Requests" with Retry-After headers (5-120 seconds based on capacity recovery estimates), X-RateLimit-* headers (Limit/Remaining/Reset) providing quota visibility enabling consumer self-throttling, X-Throttling-Reason custom headers (capacity_exceeded, quota_exceeded, circuit_breaker_open, downstream_unavailable) communicating rejection cause, **distributed coordination** using Redis for per-consumer rate limit counters with sliding window algorithm, distributed semaphores synchronizing admission across 10+ pod replicas, circuit breaker state (open/half-open/closed) coordination, and atomic Lua scripts preventing race conditions, **comprehensive observability** through Prometheus metrics (admission rate, queue depth by priority, rejection count by reason, consumer quota usage, capacity score), Grafana dashboards providing real-time throttling health visibility, and alerting rules for high rejection rates (>10%), critical queue depth (>80%), and low capacity scores (<20). Implementation leverages Azure API Management gateway-level throttling, .NET Polly RateLimiterPolicy for service-level admission control, Redis Premium for distributed state, Service Bus for optional async queuing, and capacity monitoring background service tracking resource utilization.

**When to Use:** Apply API Throttling Pattern for (1) **Variable traffic with burst potential**: Open enrollment spikes (large traffic increases from baseline), provider credentialing deadline surges, month-end billing increases, state reporting batch jobs, integration partner synchronized processing windows; (2) **Resource-constrained services**: Database connection pool limits requiring admission control, CPU-intensive processing (eligibility calculations, claims pricing engines), memory-intensive operations (large dataset queries, report generation), downstream vendor APIs with contractual rate limits; (3) **Multi-tenant platforms requiring fairness**: Shared FHIR APIs serving multiple states requiring per-state quotas preventing high-volume states from impacting low-volume states, provider APIs requiring per-provider limits ensuring small practices equal access as large health systems, partner integration APIs requiring per-partner throttling preventing misbehaving integrations impacting others; (4) **Downstream dependency protection**: Third-party drug database APIs with strict rate limits, clearinghouse submission APIs with processing quotas, state MMIS legacy systems with limited concurrent connection support, external identity providers with authentication rate limits; (5) **SLA guarantee requirements**: APIs with 99.9% uptime commitments, P95 latency targets, and error rate commitments. Avoid for synchronous real-time APIs requiring immediate response where horizontal scaling is more appropriate, extremely time-sensitive emergency workflows where queuing is unacceptable (provide dedicated capacity instead), or predictable steady traffic well below capacity (use rate limiting for abuse prevention only).

**Key Benefits:** (1) **Service stability**: Prevents resource exhaustion eliminating production incidents from memory exhaustion, database connection pool failures, and CPU saturation; maintains predictable P95 <2s latency vs multi-second spikes without throttling; prevents cascade failures where overloaded services impact dependencies; achieves target SLA availability; (2) **Fair resource allocation**: Per-consumer quotas prevent high-volume monopolization; per-state quotas ensure high-population states don't starve low-population states; priority queuing ensures critical workflows bypass throttling while bulk operations absorb delays; eliminates noisy neighbor problems; (3) **Graceful degradation**: Queuing absorbs transient spikes without request loss vs immediate failure; intelligent backpressure through Retry-After headers enables consumer retry vs aggressive retry storms worsening overload; progressive throttling vs sudden threshold failures; maintains partial functionality under extreme load; (4) **Downstream protection**: Matches upstream admission to downstream capacity preventing vendor API violations; prevents database connection pool exhaustion through semaphore-based admission; protects legacy systems with limited capacity; circuit breaker integration stops admission when downstream unavailable; (5) **Observability**: Comprehensive Prometheus metrics enable proactive capacity management; throttling metrics provide early warning before resource exhaustion; per-consumer metrics identify misbehaving integrations; reduced MTTR through metrics-driven troubleshooting.

**Implementation Complexity:** High—requires comprehensive capacity monitoring (CPU/memory/database connections with 5-second polling), distributed state coordination using Redis Premium (rate limit counters, semaphores, circuit breaker state with Lua scripts), sophisticated admission control logic (priority classification, quota management, queue coordination), request queuing infrastructure (bounded depth 5,000, priority tiers P0-P3, TTL management), extensive observability (Prometheus metrics with 15+ metric types, Grafana dashboards, alert rules), and operational procedures (4 detailed runbooks for incident response, capacity scaling, queue management, circuit breaker coordination). Development: 3-4 weeks (Week 1-2: capacity baseline through load testing, design throttling thresholds, configure Redis and monitoring; Week 3: implement middleware/policies, capacity monitoring, admission control; Week 4: load testing validation, A/B testing with 5-10% traffic, staged production rollout 10% → 50% → 100% with monitoring, consumer communication). Prerequisites: Azure infrastructure (AKS 1.25+, API Management Standard/Premium, Redis Premium P1, Service Bus optional), .NET 8 SDK with Polly 8.0+ resilience policies, Prometheus/Grafana observability stack, established capacity baselines from load testing, team skills in async programming and resilience patterns. Operational readiness: Runbooks for incident response, monitoring dashboards configured pre-deployment, alert rules for critical metrics, on-call training on throttling troubleshooting. Reusable components available: Throttling middleware, capacity monitor background service, Redis coordination scripts, reference Grafana dashboards reduce per-service effort to 1-2 weeks.

**Prerequisites:** (1) **Technical**: Azure Kubernetes Service 1.25+ with autoscaling, Azure API Management Standard/Premium for gateway throttling, Azure Cache for Redis Premium P1 (6GB, 20K ops/sec) for distributed state, Polly 8.0+ NuGet resilience policies (RateLimiterPolicy, CircuitBreakerPolicy), Prometheus 2.40+ for metrics, Grafana 9.0+ for dashboards, Application Insights for distributed tracing; (2) **Capacity baseline**: Load testing establishing sustainable RPS (e.g., 800 RPS), burst capacity before degradation (1,200 RPS), breaking point causing failures (1,800 RPS), resource utilization thresholds (CPU <75%, memory <80%, connections <80%), P95/P99 latency targets under load, documented bottlenecks; (3) **Organizational**: Team skills in rate limiting algorithms (token bucket, sliding window), async/await concurrent programming, Polly resilience patterns, HTTP status codes RFC 6585, capacity planning and load testing; Consumer coordination including communication plan for throttling rollout, documented retry strategies, consumer testing in pre-production, phased deployment with notifications; Operational readiness with runbooks for investigating high rejection rates/adjusting thresholds/managing queue depth/coordinating circuit breakers, Grafana dashboards showing admission/capacity/queue/consumer metrics, alert rules for rejection rate >10%/queue depth >80%/capacity score <20, on-call team trained on throttling troubleshooting.

**Real-World Results:** Validated implementations demonstrate: (1) **Provider Portal Claims API**: Month-end spikes that previously caused database connection pool exhaustion and high error rates are handled gracefully with throttling—the large majority of requests are admitted immediately, a portion queued with short wait times, and a small fraction rejected with intelligent retry guidance. Zero connection exhaustion incidents, sustained P95 latency within SLA targets, eliminated manual claim resubmissions; (2) **FHIR Multi-Tenant APIs**: High-volume state batch jobs that previously overwhelmed shared database capacity and degraded low-volume state APIs are controlled through per-state quotas—small states maintain consistent sub-second response times regardless of other states' load, and shared capacity is utilized efficiently; (3) **Pharmacy Drug Database API**: Unthrottled formulary change periods previously violated vendor contractual rate limits; upstream throttling with cache integration eliminates overage charges and queues burst traffic with tolerable delay; (4) **Overall Impact**: Resource exhaustion incidents eliminated, noisy neighbor incidents eliminated, faster incident response through metrics-driven troubleshooting, high request success rates maintained under peak load, SLA compliance achieved.

**Related Patterns:** Rate Limiting PTN-SEC-RATELIMIT-002 (complementary abuse prevention with fixed quotas vs capacity-aware admission), Circuit Breaker PTN-RESIL-CIRCUITBREAKER-002 (required dependency for downstream health coordination), Bulkhead PTN-RESIL-BULKHEAD-004 (resource isolation complementing admission control), Retry PTN-RESIL-RETRY-003 (consumer-side complement respecting backpressure signals), Queue-Based Load Leveling PTN-INT-QUEUELOADLEVEL-005 (alternative for longer-delay batch operations), Backpressure PTN-RESIL-BACKPRESSURE-006 (throttling implements HTTP-based backpressure), Priority Queue PTN-PERF-PRIORITYQUEUE-007 (multi-tier priority implementation), Cache-Aside PTN-PERF-CACHEASIDE-001 (reduces load requiring throttling protection), API Gateway PTN-INT-APIGATEWAY-008 (infrastructure for centralized throttling policies), Saga PTN-INT-SAGA-009 (compensation operations require priority during overload).
